NYPD Shooting Incident Report

Sri

2026-09-22

Why should you care?

Every row in this data is a person who was shot. I wanted to see when and where it happens in New York City, and what makes a shooting more likely to be deadly, so that help can go where it’s needed most.

Import

The data comes from NYC Open Data and is called the NYPD Shooting Incident Data.

url <- "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/api/v3/views/833y-fsy8/export.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD"
raw <- read_csv(url)
head(raw)
## # A tibble: 6 × 21
##   INCIDENT_KEY OCCUR_DATE OCCUR_TIME BORO     LOC_OF_OCCUR_DESC PRECINCT
##          <dbl> <chr>      <time>     <chr>    <chr>                <dbl>

## 2    298699604 12/31/2024 19:16      BROOKLYN OUTSIDE                 69
## 3    298672096 12/30/2024 16:45      BRONX    OUTSIDE                 47
## 4    298672094 12/30/2024 12:15      BRONX    OUTSIDE                 52

Tidying the data

# Keep the columns I need
shootings <- raw %>%
  select(OCCUR_DATE, OCCUR_TIME, BORO, STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG,
         VIC_AGE_GROUP)

# fix the date (it is written month/day/year)
shootings <- shootings %>%
  mutate(date = mdy(OCCUR_DATE))

# get the year and the hour of the day
shootings <- shootings %>%
  mutate(year = year(date),
         hour = hour(hms(as.character(OCCUR_TIME))))

# murder flag as TRUE/FALSE
shootings <- shootings %>%
  mutate(murder = as.logical(STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG))

# keep only valid victim age groups
valid_ages <- c("<18", "18-24", "25-44", "45-64", "65+")
shootings <- shootings %>%
  filter(VIC_AGE_GROUP %in% valid_ages)

# Make the borough names look nicer and age groups appear in order
shootings <- shootings %>%
  mutate(boro = str_to_title(BORO),
         VIC_AGE_GROUP = factor(VIC_AGE_GROUP, levels = valid_ages))

summary(shootings %>% select(date, hour, murder))
##       date                 hour        murder       
##  Min.   :2006-01-01   Min.   : 0.0   Mode :logical  
##  1st Qu.:2009-10-30   1st Qu.: 3.0   FALSE:23925    
##  Median :2014-03-26   Median :15.0   TRUE :5750     
##  Mean   :2014-11-01   Mean   :12.3                  
##  3rd Qu.:2020-06-30   3rd Qu.:20.0                  
##  Max.   :2024-12-31   Max.   :23.0

After cleaning, there are 29675 rows from 2006 to 2024. Each row is a victim, so an incident with two victims appears twice.

nrow(raw) - nrow(shootings)
## [1] 69

These are the number of rows dropped because of impossible victim ages (typos in the data).

Analysis

Looking at this data, I wanted to find out:

  1. How has the number of shootings changed over the years?
  2. When do shootings happen?
  3. How often does a shooting end in a death, and who is most at risk?
  4. After the jump in 2020, were shootings also more likely to be fatal?

Visualization 1: Shootings by year and borough

by_year <- shootings %>%
  group_by(year, boro) %>%
  summarise(victims = n())

ggplot(by_year, aes(x = year, y = victims, color = boro)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Shooting victims per year by borough",
       x = "Year", y = "Number of victims", color = "Borough")

Shootings fell for most of the 2010s, then jumped sharply in 2020 and dropped again afterward. Brooklyn had the most victims in most years, followed by the Bronx, and Staten Island had the fewest. In 2021 the Bronx passed Brooklyn for the first time in this chart. These are just counts, not rates.Bigger boroughs naturally have more shootings.

Visualization 2: When do shootings happen? (Heat map)

Each square is one hour of one weekday. Darker squares mean more shooting victims.

shootings <- shootings %>%
  mutate(weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1))

by_hour_weekday <- shootings %>%
  group_by(weekday, hour) %>%
  summarise(victims = n())

by_hour_weekday$weekday <- factor(by_hour_weekday$weekday,
                                  levels = c("Sun", "Sat", "Fri", "Thu", "Wed", "Tue", "Mon"))

ggplot(by_hour_weekday, aes(x = hour, y = weekday, fill = victims)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "red") +
  labs(title = "Shooting victims by hour and day of the week",
       x = "Hour (0 = midnight, 23 = 11 pm)", y = "Day of the week",
       fill = "Victims")

Most shootings happen late at night, especially on weekends. Weekday mornings are the quietest time.

Visualization 3: Fatal percentage by age

fatal_by_age <- shootings %>%
  group_by(VIC_AGE_GROUP) %>%
  summarise(percent_fatal = mean(murder) * 100)

ggplot(fatal_by_age, aes(x = VIC_AGE_GROUP, y = percent_fatal)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Percent of shootings that were fatal, by victim age group",
       x = "Victim age group", y = "Percent fatal")

The older the victim, the more likely the shooting is fatal.

fatal_by_age %>%
  mutate(percent_fatal = round(percent_fatal, 1))
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##   VIC_AGE_GROUP percent_fatal
##   <fct>                 <dbl>
## 1 <18                    13.2
## 2 18-24                  16.6
## 3 25-44                  21.9
## 4 45-64                  25.2
## 5 65+                    30.5
shootings %>%
  group_by(murder) %>%
  summarise(victims = n()) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(victims / sum(victims) * 100, 1))
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   murder victims percent
##   <lgl>    <int>   <dbl>
## 1 FALSE    23925    80.6
## 2 TRUE      5750    19.4

About 19.4% of shooting victims in this data died (5,750 out of 29,675), which is roughly 1 in 5. So most victims survive, but the chance of dying isn’t the same for everyone. The chart above shows it rises with age. After the jump in shootings in 2020, did the chance of dying also go up?

Model:

My line chart from Visualization 1 showed a big jump in shootings in 2020. So, I wanted to know if those shootings were more likely to be fatal.

model_data <- shootings %>%
  mutate(night = hour >= 20 | hour <= 5,
         after2020 = year >= 2020)

I made two new yes/no columns. night is TRUE if the shooting happened between 8 PM and 5 AM. after2020 is TRUE if the shooting happened in 2020 or later. The model uses these as predictors.

model_2020 <- glm(murder ~ VIC_AGE_GROUP + night + after2020,
                  data = model_data, family = binomial)
summary(model_2020)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = murder ~ VIC_AGE_GROUP + night + after2020, family = binomial, 
##     data = model_data)
## 
## Coefficients:
##                     Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)        -1.797159   0.056692 -31.700  < 2e-16 ***
## VIC_AGE_GROUP18-24  0.273582   0.059248   4.618 3.88e-06 ***
## VIC_AGE_GROUP25-44  0.616958   0.057221  10.782  < 2e-16 ***
## VIC_AGE_GROUP45-64  0.784984   0.073147  10.732  < 2e-16 ***
## VIC_AGE_GROUP65+    1.018546   0.151414   6.727 1.73e-11 ***
## nightTRUE          -0.139414   0.030807  -4.525 6.03e-06 ***
## after2020TRUE      -0.002784   0.033142  -0.084    0.933    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 29179  on 29674  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance: 28909  on 29668  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 28923
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4

I built the model with glm. It looks at every victim and learns how age, night, and after 2020 are linked to whether the victim died.

How to read this table: Each row is one predictor. The model compares everyone with a starting point (the baseline): a victim under 18, shot during the day, before 2020. That is why those three have no row.

  • Estimate: how much the predictor changes the chance of dying. Positive means more likely to die, negative means less likely.
  • Std. Error: how uncertain the estimate is. Smaller is better.
  • z value: how reliable the effect is. The further from 0, the stronger the evidence.
  • Pr(>|z|): the p-value. Under 0.05 means the effect is real and it is very unlikely to be luck.
  • Stars: a shortcut for the p-value. More stars means a stronger result.

Example: Age 65+ has a positive estimate (1.02) and a tiny p-value (1.73e-11, which is 0.0000000000173). So victims 65 and older were more likely to die than victims under 18. After 2020 has a p-value of 0.933, far above 0.05, so there is no evidence it changed anything.

The estimates are hard to read directly, so the next step turns them into plain multipliers.

round(exp(coef(model_2020)), 2)
##        (Intercept) VIC_AGE_GROUP18-24 VIC_AGE_GROUP25-44 VIC_AGE_GROUP45-64 
##               0.17               1.31               1.85               2.19 
##   VIC_AGE_GROUP65+          nightTRUE      after2020TRUE 
##               2.77               0.87               1.00

Each number compares a group with a victim under 18, shot during the day, before 2020. A number above 1 means a higher chance of dying, 1.00 means no change, and a number below 1 means a lower chance.

Summary: Shootings were not more likely to be fatal after 2020. More people were shot, but the chance of a victim dying stayed the same. Age was the clearest predictor: the older the victim, the more likely they were to die.

Conclusions

Looking back at my four questions:

  1. How has the number of shootings changed over the years? Shootings fell for most of the 2010s, jumped sharply in 2020, and then dropped again. Brooklyn and the Bronx had the most victims, but these are counts, not rates.
  2. When do shootings happen? Mostly late at night and on weekends. Weekday mornings are the quietest time.
  3. How often does a shooting end in a death, and who is most at risk? About 1 in 5 victims (19.4%) died. The older the victim, the more likely they were to die, from about 13.2% for victims under 18 to about 30.5% for victims 65 and older.
  4. After the jump in 2020, were shootings also more likely to be fatal? No. More people were shot, but the chance of a victim dying stayed the same.

Shootings in New York City are not spread evenly. They rise and fall over the years, they cluster late at night and on weekends, and older victims are far more likely to die. The jump in 2020 was about how many people were shot, not how deadly each shooting was.

Bias

Bias in the data

  • This is police data, so it only has shootings that were reported and recorded. Anything that never got reported isn’t here, and reporting could be different from one neighborhood to the next.
  • Each row is a victim, not a shooting. If two people were shot in one incident, it shows up twice.
  • A few ages were clearly typos (like “1022”), so I removed those rows, which could change the results a bit.
  • A lot of the shooter information is missing, so I didn’t use it. That means this data can’t tell us anything about who is doing the shootings.
  • There’s nothing about the injury in the data, like where the person was hit or how fast they got to a hospital which matters a lot for survival.

Bias in my analysis

  • I looked at counts, not rates. Bigger boroughs will have more shootings no matter what, so comparing boroughs by counts isn’t really fair.
  • I picked which variables to use. I left race out on purpose because this data can’t explain why any differences exist, and I didn’t want to suggest something untrue about a group.
  • I chose 2020 as the cutoff because I saw the jump in my own chart. Another year might give a different answer, and other things that changed over the years (like how shootings were recorded) aren’t in the model.
  • I decided that “night” means 8 PM to 5 AM. If I picked different hours, the result could change.
  • The model only shows what goes together, not what causes what. Older victims were more likely to die, but I can’t say why from this data.
